Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

derivations.claim: Fix $0<\ell\le1$ and put $N=\lceil1/\ell\rceil$. Since $1/\ell\le N<1/\ell+1\le2/\ell$, one has $\ell/2\le1/N\le\ell$. Partition each coordinate interval into $N$ intervals of length $1/N$, assigning endpoints by a fixed half-open convention and intersecting with $U$. Their product cells lie in side-$\ell$ cubes centered at their midpoints, which belong to the cells. Each has volume $N^{-D}\ge2^{-D}\ell^D$. On each of the $2D$ boundary faces perform the same $(D-1)$-dimensional partition. Assign shared face edges to the lowest-index incident face and then to a lowest-index neighboring cell; the grid vertices and edges have surface measure zero and lie in the closures of those cells. Each cell remains in its same closed ambient cube and its midpoint belongs to it. Its normalized surface mass is $(2D)^{-1}N^{-(D-1)}\ge(2D)^{-1}2^{-(D-1)}\ell^{D-1}$.

Every residual ball intersection has volume at most $\omega_D\rho^D$. On each face its surface intersection is contained in a $(D-1)$-dimensional ball of radius $\rho$, of measure at most $\omega_{D-1}\rho^{D-1}$. Summing over $2D$ faces and dividing by total surface area $2D$ gives boundary probability at most $\omega_{D-1}\rho^{D-1}$. The probability densities are the positive constants $1$ and $1/(2D)$ on their respective supports. These are the required upper and lower bounds with the stated small-scale range.

citations.quote: The following assertion is false under the library's bounded global Hölder norm: every bounded Lipschitz domain satisfying an exterior sphere condition at each boundary point, with a strictly elliptic operator having Hölder coefficients and nonpositive expanded zero-order coefficient, has for every Hölder forcing and continuous Dirichlet data a unique solution in $C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u$$
on $U$, where $a(x)$ is symmetric, $\xi^Ta(x)\xi\ge\lambda_0|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\lambda_0>0$, the coefficients are continuous and bounded, and $\widetilde c\le0$. There is a constant $C_L<\infty$, depending only on $U$, $\lambda_0$, and the coefficient bounds, such that every $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $L[w]\in C^0(U)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$
In particular, for any two functions $u^*,h\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$,
$$\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[u^*]-L[h]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
On every ball, $C^{2,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ therefore agrees with the finite-scaled-norm class of that dependency. This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. For coefficients $a_{ij},b_i,c_i,d$ on $U$, define the positive divergence-form operator
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_iD_i u+du.$$
When the coefficients are continuously differentiable where needed, its nondivergence expansion is
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
with
$$\widetilde b_j=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i a_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i b_i+d.$$
The **positive divergence convention** here means that the principal part is $+\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$. This sign is part of the definition.

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

derivations.claim: Write $p_j=\mu(X_j)$ and $N_j=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1_{\{Y_i\in X_j\}}$. Since $p_j\ge c\ell^s=m^{-1/2}$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$, we have $K\le\sqrt m$. Independence gives $\mathbb E e^{-N_j/2}=(1-p_j+p_je^{-1/2})^m\le\exp(-mp_j(1-e^{-1/2}))$. For a nonnegative random variable $Z$, $a\mathbb P(Z>a)\le\mathbb E Z$, by integrating $Z\ge a\mathbf1_{Z>a}$. Apply this with $Z=e^{-N_j/2}$ and $a=e^{-mp_j/4}$ to get $\mathbb P(N_j<mp_j/2)\le\exp(mp_j/4-mp_j(1-e^{-1/2}))\le e^{-mp_j/8}$. Here $e^{1/2}\ge1+1/2+1/8=13/8>8/5$ implies $e^{-1/2}<5/8$, and $1-x\le e^{-x}$ follows by differentiating $e^{-x}-1+x$.

The event $N_j<\sqrt m/2$ is contained in $N_j<mp_j/2$. By step 1.1 and [F2], its union over cells has probability at most $K e^{-\sqrt m/8}\le\sqrt m e^{-\sqrt m/8}$. This proves the probability assertion, with the trivial lower bound zero when necessary.

On the complementary event fix $x\in X_j$. Every sample $Y_i\in X_j$ is within $\delta$ of $x$. The three-term square inequality gives $|v(x)-g(x)|^2\le3|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2+3\delta^{2\alpha}([v]_{\alpha;X}^2+[g]_{\alpha;X}^2)$. Average over the $N_j\ge\sqrt m/2$ samples in this cell. Its first term is at most $(3/N_j)\sum_{i=1}^m|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2\le6\sqrt m\,m^{-1}\sum_i|v(Y_i)-g(Y_i)|^2$. Taking the supremum over $x$ proves the inequality. This is a deterministic inequality on the occupancy event, so it holds for sample-dependent trial functions as well.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: The cell measures sum to one by [F3], and each is at least $c\varepsilon^s=1/\sqrt m$. Therefore the number of cells is at most $\sqrt m$.

A fixed cell of mass $p_j\ge c\varepsilon^s=1/\sqrt m$ is missed by all $m$ independent samples with probability $(1-p_j)^m\le(1-1/\sqrt m)^m$ by [F2]. By [F1], the probability that at least one cell is missed is at most $\sqrt m(1-1/\sqrt m)^m$.

On the complementary event, every cell contains a sample. Since each cell lies in a cube of side $\varepsilon$, any point of the cell is within the cube's Euclidean diameter $\sqrt d\varepsilon$ of a sample in that same cell. Substituting $\varepsilon=(c\sqrt m)^{-1/s}$ gives the stated fill radius and probability.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

derivations.claim: If $U=\varnothing$, both spaces are zero and the conclusions hold. Otherwise choose finite $a<b$ with $U\subset\{a<x_1<b\}$. The zero extension of any $h\in H$ belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ with the same norm. Restricting the countable dense box-step family in [F1] to $U$ therefore gives a countable dense subset of $H$. The product $Z=H^{d+1}$ is a separable Hilbert space.

The map $J:H^1(U)\to Z$, $J(v)=(v,D_1v,\ldots,D_dv)$, is an isometry for the full Sobolev norm. Its range is closed: if $J(v_n)\to(v,g_1,\ldots,g_d)$ in $Z$, then for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\int vD_i\phi=\lim_n\int v_nD_i\phi=-\lim_n\int D_iv_n\phi=-\int g_i\phi$. Thus $g_i=D_iv$ weakly, so the limit is $J(v)$. A closed subspace of a Hilbert space is complete, hence $H^1(U)$ is Hilbert.

By the closure definition, $V$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(U)$ and is Hilbert. The Poincare inequality applies because $U$ is bounded in the first direction, and yields $\|Dv\|_2^2\le\|v\|_{H^1}^2\le(1+C^2)\|Dv\|_2^2$ on $V$. This proves norm equivalence and continuity of the inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$. Injectivity holds because these spaces use the same almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

A subspace $Y$ of a separable metric space $Z$ is separable under [A1]: if $(z_j)$ is dense in $Z$, the sets $Y\cap B(z_j,r)$ for positive rational $r$ form a countable base of $Y$; choose one point from every nonempty such set. Any relatively open neighborhood contains one of these sets, so the chosen points are dense. Apply this first to $J(H^1(U))\subset Z$ and then to $J(V)$; transport the dense subsets through the isometry $J$. Thus $V$ is separable.

By [F4], $C_c^\infty(U)$ is dense in $H$, and it is contained in $V$ by [F2]. Thus $V\hookrightarrow H$ is dense. The Hilbert, separability, continuity and injectivity conclusions already proved give the canonical evolution triple by [F5]. Every argument used an arbitrary bounded open $U$, so none requires a boundary chart or a polyhedral boundary.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. For coefficients $a_{ij},b_i,c_i,d$ on $U$, define the positive divergence-form operator
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d D_i\bigl(a_{ij}D_j u+b_i u\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_iD_i u+du.$$
When the coefficients are continuously differentiable where needed, its nondivergence expansion is
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
with
$$\widetilde b_j=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i a_{ij}+b_j+c_j,\qquad \widetilde c=\sum_{i=1}^dD_i b_i+d.$$
The **positive divergence convention** here means that the principal part is $+\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$. This sign is part of the definition.

By [F3], choose $\phi_n\in C_c^\infty(U)$ with $\phi_n\to e$ in $H^1(U)$. The distributional definition of each divergence term and the ordinary test-function integration by parts give
$$\int_U\phi_nL[e],dx=-\int_U a_{ij}D_j eD_i\phi_n\,dx-\int_U b_i eD_i\phi_n\,dx+\int_U c_iD_i e\,\phi_n\,dx+\int_U d e\,\phi_n\,dx.$$
All coefficients are bounded and $e,\nabla e,L[e]\in L^2$, so each term is continuous under $H^1$ convergence. Taking $n\to\infty$ and using [F2] yields
$$-\int_U eL[e],dx=\int_U a_{ij}D_j eD_i e\,dx+\int_U b_i eD_i e\,dx-\int_U c_i eD_i e\,dx-\int_U d e^2\,dx.$$
The principal term is at least $\lambda_0\|\nabla e\|_2^2$ by ellipticity.

The coefficient bound gives $\|b\|^2+\|c\|^2\le\lambda_0^2v^2$ and $|d|\le\lambda_0v^2$. Hence the absolute value of the two first-order terms is at most $\sqrt2\lambda_0v\|e\|_2\|
abla e\|_2$, and the zero-order term is at most $\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2$. Young's inequality bounds the first-order contribution by $ rac{\lambda_0}{2}\|
abla e\|_2^2+\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2$. Therefore
$$-\int_U eL[e],dx\ge rac{\lambda_0}{2}\|
abla e\|_2^2-2\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2.$$

Since $L[e]\in L^2(U)$, Cauchy–Schwarz and step 1.2 imply
$$\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\|\nabla e\|_2^2\le\|L[e]\|_2\|e\|_2+2\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2\le\frac{1}{2\lambda_0}\|L[e]\|_2^2+\left(\frac{1}{2\lambda_0}+2\lambda_0v^2\right)\|e\|_2^2.$$
Thus $\|\nabla e\|_2^2\le\lambda_0^{-2}\|L[e]\|_2^2+(\lambda_0^{-2}+4v^2)\|e\|_2^2$. By [F1], adding $\|e\|_2^2$ gives the claimed $H^1$ estimate with $C_E=\max\{\lambda_0^{-2},1+\lambda_0^{-2}+4v^2\}$.

derivations.claim: By [F3], choose $\phi_n\in C_c^\infty(U)$ with $\phi_n\to e$ in $H^1(U)$. The distributional definition of each divergence term and the ordinary test-function integration by parts give $$\int_U\phi_nL[e]\,dx=-\int_U a_{ij}D_j eD_i\phi_n\,dx-\int_U b_i eD_i\phi_n\,dx+\int_U c_iD_i e\,\phi_n\,dx+\int_U d e\,\phi_n\,dx.$$ All coefficients are bounded and $e,\nabla e,L[e]\in L^2$, so each term is continuous under $H^1$ convergence. Taking $n\to\infty$ and using [F2] yields $$-\int_U eL[e]\,dx=\int_U a_{ij}D_j eD_i e\,dx+\int_U b_i eD_i e\,dx-\int_U c_i eD_i e\,dx-\int_U d e^2\,dx.$$ The principal term is at least $\lambda_0\|\nabla e\|_2^2$ by ellipticity.

The coefficient bound gives $\|b\|^2+\|c\|^2\le\lambda_0^2v^2$ and $|d|\le\lambda_0v^2$. Hence the absolute value of the two first-order terms is at most $\sqrt2\lambda_0v\|e\|_2\|
abla e\|_2$, and the zero-order term is at most $\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2$. Young's inequality bounds the first-order contribution by $ rac{\lambda_0}{2}\|
abla e\|_2^2+\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2$. Therefore $$-\int_U eL[e]\,dx\ge rac{\lambda_0}{2}\|
abla e\|_2^2-2\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2.$$

Since $L[e]\in L^2(U)$, Cauchy–Schwarz and step 2.1 imply $$\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\|\nabla e\|_2^2\le\|L[e]\|_2\|e\|_2+2\lambda_0v^2\|e\|_2^2\le\frac{1}{2\lambda_0}\|L[e]\|_2^2+\left(\frac{1}{2\lambda_0}+2\lambda_0v^2\right)\|e\|_2^2.$$ Thus $\|\nabla e\|_2^2\le\lambda_0^{-2}\|L[e]\|_2^2+(\lambda_0^{-2}+4v^2)\|e\|_2^2$. By [F1], adding $\|e\|_2^2$ gives the claimed $H^1$ estimate with $C_E=\max\{\lambda_0^{-2},1+\lambda_0^{-2}+4v^2\}$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $t>0$: (i) $\Gamma(\cdot,t)>0$
and $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\,dx=1$; (ii) parabolic scaling:
$\Gamma(\lambda x,\lambda^2t)=\lambda^{-n}\Gamma(x,t)$ for every $\lambda>0$ and
$x\in\mathbb R^n$; (iii) $\Gamma$ is $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)$ and solves the heat equation there,
$\partial_t\Gamma(x,t)=\Delta_x\Gamma(x,t)$; (iv) for every multi-index $\alpha$
there is $C_{n,\alpha}<\infty$ with
$|D^\alpha_x\Gamma(x,t)|\le C_{n,\alpha}t^{-(|\alpha|+n)/2}e^{-|x|^2/(8t)}$ for
all $x\in\mathbb R^n$, $t>0$; in particular $\|\Gamma(\cdot,t)\|_1=1$ and
$(\Gamma(\cdot,t))_{t>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity on $\mathbb R^n$.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$, and let $\Gamma$ be the causal
extension of the heat kernel. Then
$\Gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^{n+1})$, and its regular distribution
$u_\Gamma\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^{n+1})$ satisfies
$(\partial_t-\Delta)u_\Gamma=\delta_{(0,0)}$, that is,
$$\langle(\partial_t-\Delta)u_\Gamma,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(0,0)\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{n+1}),$$
so the causal extension is a fundamental solution of $\partial_t-\Delta$.
Moreover $\Gamma(\cdot,t)\to\delta_0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ as
$t\downarrow0^+$, that is, $\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Gamma(x,t)\varphi(x)\,dx\to\varphi(0)$
for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$. The derivative $\partial_t$ is
the distributional derivative in the last space-time coordinate.

If $K\subseteq U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq U$.

derivations.claim: Fix a constant symmetric matrix $A_0$ with eigenvalues in $[\lambda,\Lambda]$. The linear substitution $x=A_0^{1/2}y$ in [F1] gives $$G(x,t)=\mathbf1_{t>0}(4\pi t)^{-d/2}(\det A_0)^{-1/2}\exp\bigl(-x^TA_0^{-1}x/(4t)\bigr),\qquad (\partial_t-A_0:D^2)G=\delta.$$ Put $N=d+2$ and $K_{ij}=D_{ij}G$. Direct differentiation gives $|K_{ij}(z)|\le C\rho(z,0)^{-N}$, $|D_xK_{ij}(z)|\le C\rho(z,0)^{-N-1}$ and $|\partial_tK_{ij}(z)|\le C\rho(z,0)^{-N-2}$ away from zero, with Gaussian decay as $|x|/\sqrt t$ increases. The extension across $t=0$ is smooth away from $x=0$, since that decay dominates every power. The constants are uniform over $A_0$ in the given ellipticity interval.

For use with cutoffs, the following interpolation estimate holds on nested cylinders, with norms scaled to their outer radius $r$: for each $\varepsilon>0$, the scaled lower-order $\alpha$ norms of $u$ and $rDu$ are at most $\varepsilon r^2(\|D^2u\|_{\alpha;r}+\|u_t\|_{\alpha;r})+C_\varepsilon\|u\|_\infty$, provided the finite difference segments lie in the larger cylinder. To verify it, write $D_iu(x,t)$ as a centered first difference of step $\theta r$ plus its Taylor integral remainder, bounded by $C\theta r\|D^2u\|_\infty$. Apply the same identity to differences between two points. For separations smaller than $\theta r$ use the top Hölder norms, and for larger separations use the supremum estimate and divide by the separation to the power $\alpha$. For time differences of $u$ use $|t-s|\|u_t\|_\infty$. For time differences of $Du$ use spatial first differences of step $\sqrt{|t-s|}$, bounding their time difference by $C\sqrt{|t-s|}\|u_t\|_\infty$ and the two remainders by $C\sqrt{|t-s|}\|D^2u\|_\infty$; then split at $|t-s|=\theta^2r^2$. The coefficients of the top norms are positive powers of $\theta$ because $\alpha<1$. Choosing $\theta$ small makes them at most $\varepsilon$; the larger-separation terms have finite constants depending on that $\theta$ and the cylinder separation.

Each positive-time spatial integral of $K_{ij}$ is zero. Its improper integrals on parabolic balls have a bound independent of the radius. Indeed integration of $D_{ij}G$ over $|x|<R$ gives a boundary integral of $D_jG$; its absolute value is at most $CR^dt^{-d/2-1}\exp(-cR^2/t)$. Integration for $0<t<R^2$, followed by $t=R^2s$, is bounded by $C\int_0^1s^{-d/2-1}e^{-c/s}ds<\infty$. The integral is independent of $R$ by scaling. Differences of two such truncations, hence the integrals on centered parabolic annuli, are bounded uniformly as well. This is the cancellation needed at the singularity; an absolute integral of $|K_{ij}|$ there is not asserted.

Let $v\in C_c^\infty$ have support in a parabolic cylinder of radius at most $r$ and put $F_0=v_t-A_0:D^2v$. Integrating the derivative of the Gaussian convolution from a time before the support gives $v=G*F_0$: the initial convolution is zero, its derivative is convolution with $F_0$, and the positive-time approximate identity gives the upper endpoint. This uses only [F1] and differentiation of smooth compactly supported functions. Differentiation of this identity expresses $D_{ij}v$ as the principal-value convolution with $K_{ij}$, with a fixed bounded constant multiple of $F_0$ if the truncation is by parabolic balls rather than positive time strips. That constant is the radius-independent truncation integral in step 2.1.

The singular-integral estimates follow directly as follows. At a pole subtract $F_0$ evaluated at that pole. On an annulus of radius $s$, the difference is bounded by $[F_0]_\alpha s^\alpha$, and its absolute integral against $K_{ij}$ is at most $C[F_0]_\alpha s^\alpha$. For two poles at parabolic distance $h$, the parts within distance $4h$ of either pole are therefore bounded by $C[F_0]_\alpha\int_0^{4h}s^{\alpha-1}ds\le C[F_0]_\alpha h^\alpha$. On the complement use the same subtracted constant at both poles. The kernel difference is at most $Chs^{-N-1}$: spatial displacement follows from $D_xK_{ij}$, and time displacement, of size at most $h^2$, from $\partial_tK_{ij}$ and $h^2s^{-N-2}\le hs^{-N-1}$. Its integral is bounded by $C[F_0]_\alpha h\int_{4h}^\infty s^{\alpha-2}ds\le C[F_0]_\alpha h^\alpha$. Changing the near-region truncation produces annular pieces controlled by these same estimates; changing the subtracted constant produces at most $C|F_0(z)-F_0(z')|$ by step 2.1. Thus $[D^2v]_\alpha\le C[F_0]_\alpha$. On the support neighborhood, integrating only up to radius comparable with $r$ and using the bounded truncation term gives $\|D^2v\|_\infty\le C(\|F_0\|_\infty+r^\alpha[F_0]_\alpha)$; outside that neighborhood the kernel is nonsingular and its Gaussian bound gives the same estimate. The compact time support may be used to truncate all time integrals before subtraction, so no absolutely divergent integral at infinite time is introduced.

Since $v_t=F_0+A_0:D^2v$, the same bounds hold for $v_t$. In the scaled notation $\|g\|_{\alpha;r}=\|g\|_\infty+r^\alpha[g]_\alpha$, the result is $$r^2\bigl(\|D^2v\|_{\alpha;r}+\|v_t\|_{\alpha;r}\bigr)\le Cr^2\|v_t-A_0:D^2v\|_{\alpha;r}.$$ All constants depend only on $d,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the fixed support-radius multiple. The strict inequality $\alpha<1$ is used in the convergent far integral of step 4.1.

Choose a cutoff $\eta$ supported in a cylinder of radius $r$ near $z_0$, and put $v=\eta u$, extended by zero. Freeze $A_0=A(z_0)$. Leibniz's formula gives $$v_t-A_0:D^2v=\eta F+(A-A_0):D^2v+\beta\cdot Dv+qv+u(\eta_t-A:D^2\eta-\beta\cdot D\eta)-2(A D\eta)\cdot Du.$$ The scaled product norm of $(A-A_0):D^2v$ is bounded by $Cr^\alpha[A]_\alpha\|D^2v\|_{\alpha;r}$. Choose $r$ so that this coefficient, multiplied by the constant in step 5.1, is at most $1/4$, and absorb it there. The remaining drift, zero-order and cutoff terms involve only $u,Du$ and $F$; step 1.2 absorbs their top-norm contributions after choosing its $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small. Cutoffs with derivatives bounded by powers of the inverse gap between inner and outer cylinders are supplied by [F2] after rescaling.

The resulting nested-cylinder inequality has the form $M(s)\le\varepsilon M(S)+C_\varepsilon(S-s)^{-m}B$, where $M$ is the full scaled top norm, $m<\infty$ is fixed and $B=\|u\|_\infty+\|F\|_\alpha$. To remove the outer top norm, choose radii $s_j=s_0+a(1-2^{-j})$ whose limiting cylinder is strictly inside the domain, and take $\varepsilon<2^{-m-1}$. Iteration gives a convergent geometric sum of the $B$ terms. The remainder $\varepsilon^jM(s_j)$ tends to zero because $u$ is smooth on the fixed larger compact cylinder. Thus $M(s_0)\le CB$. A finite cover of $K$ by the small cylinders in step 6.1, and step 1.2 for the lower derivatives, gives the stated estimate. The choices used coefficient Hölder bounds and ellipticity only, proving the asserted independence from higher coefficient derivatives.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $d\ge1$, and put $H=L^2(U;\mathbb R)$ and $V=H^1_0(U;\mathbb R)$, where the latter is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(U)$. Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, its inclusion into $H$ is continuous, injective and dense, and $(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple. The gradient norm and the full $H^1$ norm are equivalent on $V$. No regularity of $\partial U$ is required.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $V$ be a separable real Hilbert
space, and let $(V,H,V^*)$ be its real evolution triple. Suppose
$a(t;\cdot,\cdot):V\times V\to\mathbb R$ is bilinear and scalar measurable
for each fixed pair $v,w\in V$, and there is one null set outside which
$$|a(t;v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad a(t;v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$$
for all $v,w\in V$, with constants $M>0$ and $\alpha>0$. Let
$f\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ and $u_0\in H$. Then there is a unique
$u\in W(0,T;V)$ with $u(0)=u_0$ and, for almost every $t$,
$$\langle u'(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}+a(t;u(t),v) =\langle f(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\qquad(v\in V).$$
For every $t\in[0,T]$ it satisfies
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2+\alpha\int_0^t\|u(s)\|_V^2\,ds \le\|u_0\|_H^2+\alpha^{-1}\int_0^t\|f(s)\|_{V^*}^2\,ds.$$
The proof applies BNB to the space-time form. Scalar measurability suffices
because $V$ is separable and the measurable inverse action is proved locally.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice together with the Axiom of Choice, inherited through the published ACL characterisation and the chain-rule interfaces cited below. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $u\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $k\in\mathbb R$, and put $u_k:=(u-k)^+$ and $u^-_k:=(u-k)^-$ on measurable representatives.
Then $u_k,u^-_k\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with
$$Du_k=\mathbf 1_{\{u>k\}}Du,\qquad Du^-_k=-\mathbf 1_{\{u<k\}}Du\qquad\text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
and $Du_k=0$ a.e. on $\{u\le k\}$. If $|\Omega|<\infty$, then $u_k,u^-_k\in H^1(\Omega)$; more generally, either truncation belongs to $H^1(\Omega)$ whenever that truncation is in $L^2(\Omega)$. In particular, $u_k\in H^1(\Omega)$ for $k\ge0$, and $u^-_k\in H^1(\Omega)$ for $k\le0$. If $n\ge2$, $\Omega$ is bounded and $C^1$, and $u_k\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then this membership is the boundary condition $u\le k$ on $\partial\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]]. For every $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ the product $\eta^2u_k$ lies in $H^1_0(\Omega)$ with
$$D(\eta^2u_k)=2\eta u_k\,D\eta+\eta^2Du_k\qquad\text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
so $\eta^2u_k$ belongs to the Sobolev test space. It is admissible in the global $H^{-1}$ formulation when the source pairing is continuous; for a local inequality with $f\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$, its pairing extends by density on a bounded neighborhood of the cutoff support. No pairing with a general $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ source and an arbitrary $H^1_0$ test is asserted. The same membership conclusions hold for $k$-translates of $u^+$ and for the cut-off functions $\eta^2u_k$ with $\eta\in W^{1,\infty}_c(\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$;
write $\delta_hu=(\delta_h^1u,\dots,\delta_h^nu)$ and
$Du=(D_1u,\dots,D_nu)$ for the difference-quotient and gradient vectors, with
$$\|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|\delta_h^iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega')},\qquad \|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}:=\Big\|\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iu|^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
(1) If $1\le p\le\infty$ and $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then for every
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)$ and every coordinate
direction $i$,
$$\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|\delta_hu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le n^{|1/p-1/2|}\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)} .$$
At $p=2$ the vector estimate has constant one. The coordinate bound also
holds on any open $U\subseteq\Omega$ for a fixed $i,h$ for which every
segment $[x,x+he_i]$, $x\in U$, stays in $\Omega$; compact containment
is unnecessary. In particular, $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(H)}\le
\|D_iu\|_{L^p(H)}$ for tangential directions on a half-space $H$.
(2) Conversely, if $1<p<\infty$, $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and there is $C$
with $\|\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$ for every coordinate $i$ and all
$0<|h|<\operatorname{dist}(\Omega',\partial\Omega)/2$, then
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega')$ with $D_iu\in L^p(\Omega')$,
$\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega')}\le C$, and
$\delta_h^iu\rightharpoonup D_iu$ weakly in $L^p(\Omega')$ as $h\to0$.
For $1\le p<\infty$, tangential quotients on $H$ also converge strongly:
$\delta_h^iu\to D_iu$ in $L^p(H)$ as $h\to0$.
Both parts are identities of classes and hold without any regularity of
$\partial\Omega$. At $p=1$ the converse in (2) is deliberately not asserted;
the companion remark records why only a measure derivative survives there.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge2$. For every integer $k\ge0$ and
$1\le p\le\infty$, there is a bounded linear operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(\widehat S_d)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^d)$$
whose restriction to $\widehat S_d$ is the input class. Consequently
$\widehat S_d$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension domain in the sense of
[[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]. The operator may
be chosen with support in one fixed bounded set.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $0<\alpha<1$, and let $O\subset\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$ be open. Use $\rho((x,t),(y,s))=\max\{|x-y|,\sqrt{|t-s|}\}$ and $[v]_{\alpha;E}=\sup_{z\ne z'\in E}|v(z)-v(z')|/\rho(z,z')^\alpha$. Suppose the symmetric matrix $A$, vector $\beta$ and scalar $q$ are locally $\alpha$-Hölder for this metric, and $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ with $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$. For every compact parabolic cylinder $K$ contained in the interior of a larger compact cylinder $K'\subset O$ there is $C<\infty$, depending on these cylinders, $d,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the coefficient Hölder norms on $K'$, such that every smooth $u$ satisfying $u_t-A:D^2u-\beta\cdot Du-qu=F$ near $K'$ obeys
$$\|u\|_{C^{2+\alpha,1+\alpha/2}(K)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{L^\infty(K')}+\|F\|_{C^{\alpha,\alpha/2}(K')}\bigr).$$
Here the left norm consists of the suprema and parabolic $\alpha$-Hölder seminorms of $u,Du,D^2u,u_t$. The constant does not depend on derivatives of the coefficients above their displayed Hölder regularity. The assertion is an estimate for smooth solutions, not a prior assumption of classical solvability.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $\mathcal F\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$. Its closure in the supremum metric is compact if and only if $\mathcal F$ is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded.

derivations.claim: Write $P=-\partial_t+A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+q$. First prove classical comparison. If $Pv\ge0$ and $v\le0$ on the initial and lateral faces, fix $\tau<T$. The function $v-\varepsilon(t+1)$ has strictly positive $P$, since $P(t+1)=-1+q(t+1)\le-1$. If it had a positive maximum on $\bar U\times[0,\tau]$, that maximum would occur at a spatial interior point at time $s>0$. Its spatial gradient is zero, its Hessian is negative semidefinite, and its time derivative is nonnegative if $s=\tau$ and zero if $s<\tau$. The derivatives exist since $\tau<T$. Thus its $P$ value is nonpositive, a contradiction. Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, then $\tau\uparrow T$, using continuity. The same proof works on subcylinders and shows uniqueness by applying it to both signs of a solution difference.

For a smooth-coefficient weak subsolution of $v_t-\operatorname{div}(A Dv)-B\cdot Dv-qv\le0$ with zero initial positive part and weak nonpositive boundary order, use $v_+$ as test. The needed time identity follows by taking time averages in the variational equation, testing with smooth convex approximations to the positive part, applying the ordinary chain rule to those averages, and passing first in the averaging radius and then in the convex approximation; the derivatives of the convex approximations lie in $[0,1]$, so [F3] and dominated convergence justify both passages. Consequently $$\frac12\frac d{dt}\|v_+\|_2^2+\frac\lambda2\|Dv_+\|_2^2\le\left(\frac{\|B\|_\infty^2}{2\lambda}+\|q_+\|_\infty\right)\|v_+\|_2^2.$$ An integrating factor and its zero initial value give $v_+=0$. To justify weak boundary order without a smooth boundary, write $v=w+H$ with $w\in H^1_0(D)$ and compare to a smooth barrier $W$ satisfying $H-W<0$ on a neighborhood of $\partial D$. Approximate $w$ by compactly supported smooth $w_j$. Then $(w_j+H-W)_+$ has compact support in $D$. The positive-part map is continuous in $H^1$: its gradient formula from [F3], the vanishing of $Dv$ on a zero level set, and dominated convergence along almost-everywhere convergent subsequences prove this directly. Thus $(v-W)_+\in H^1_0(D)$. Replace $W$ by $W+\varepsilon$ and then let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ when boundary order is non-strict. This proves the same local comparison on intersections with an interior ball, using the classical interior values on its artificial boundary.

Enlarge the time interval slightly. At each interior spatial point the coefficients and $f$ have one-sided Hölder limits at $T$ by hypothesis; extend them constantly after $T$, preserving ellipticity, sign and bounds. Extend the lateral datum continuously after $T$. It suffices to construct a solution on the longer cylinder and then restrict, so all subsequent compact-interior arguments include the original final face. Choose finite unions $U_n$ of dyadic cubes compactly contained in $U$, whose distance from its complement is at least $2/n$, exhausting every compact subset of $U$, and with every point of $\partial U_n$ within $C/n$ of $\partial U$. For example use a grid with side at most $1/(10n\sqrt d)$ and take the interior of the union of closed grid cubes at distance greater than $3/n$ from the complement, passing to increasing finite unions with earlier domains if needed. Neighboring excluded cubes show the stated boundary-distance bound. Every fixed compact subset is eventually included.

Extend $A$ outside $U$ by $\lambda I$, and $\beta,q,f$ by zero, using bounded measurable extensions also before the initial time. Convolve with nonnegative smooth mollifiers of spatial radius less than $1/n$ and time radius less than $1/n^2$. The smooth coefficients $A_n,\beta_n,q_n,f_n$ retain the uniform bounds, ellipticity and $q_n\le0$, converge locally in every lower Hölder exponent, and have uniformly bounded local $\alpha$ norms away from the initial/lateral boundary. The last assertion follows directly by writing a difference of convolutions as the average of the corresponding differences of the original locally Hölder function. Extend the continuous combined datum to a continuous $H$ on a neighborhood of the closed cylinder and mollify it to $H_n\to H$ uniformly. Such an extension can be made explicitly with a continuous increasing subadditive modulus $\omega$ dominating the data modulus: $H(z)=\inf_{y\in\Gamma_T}(\psi(y)+\omega(d_p(z,y)))$, truncated to the data range, equals $\psi$ on $\Gamma_T$ and has modulus $\omega$. A concave dominating modulus is subadditive. Prescribe $H_n$ on $\partial U_n$ and initially on $U_n$.

Rewrite the smooth nondivergence equation in divergence form, with $B_n=\beta_n-\operatorname{div}A_n$. Subtract $H_n$ and multiply the zero-data unknown by $e^{-k_nt}$, choosing finite $k_n$ large enough that its form satisfies $a_n(v,v)+k_n\|v\|_2^2\ge(\lambda/2)\|Dv\|_2^2+\|v\|_2^2$. This follows by Young's inequality for the finite bounded $B_n$ and $q_n$; the form is bounded for each fixed $n$. The transformed source is smooth and belongs to $L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(U_n))$. Apply [F1] and [F2], and undo the transformations, to get a weak solution $u_n$ with those initial and lateral data. The bounds on $B_n$, $k_n$ and derivatives of $H_n$ need not be uniform: they were used only to construct each approximant. Weak comparison from step 1.2 with $\pm(M_0+tM_f)$, where $M_0$ bounds $|H_n|$ and $M_f$ bounds $|f_n|$, gives $|u_n|\le M_0+tM_f$, uniformly in $n$.

Fix $x_0\in\partial U$. Take an exterior ball of center $y$ and radius $R$. Replacing it by a smaller internally tangent ball makes its only contact with the old sphere be $x_0$; its remaining points lie in the old ball's interior, so its only contact with $\bar U$ is $x_0$. For $r=|x-y|$ set $h=R^{-p}-r^{-p}\ge0$ on $\bar U$, with $h(x_0)=0$. Direct differentiation gives $$L_nh=pr^{-p-2}\left(\operatorname{tr}A_n-(p+2)\frac{(x-y)^TA_n(x-y)}{r^2}+\beta_n\cdot(x-y)\right)+q_nh.$$ Choose $p$ with $(p+2)\lambda>d\Lambda+\sup_n\|\beta_n\|_\infty(R+\rho)+1$. Multiply $h$ by a positive constant so that $-L_nh\ge1$ in $U_n\cap B_\rho(x_0)$, uniformly in $n$. On the artificial sphere $\bar U\cap\partial B_\rho(x_0)$ the minimum of $h$ is positive by its isolated zero. These barriers use coefficient bounds and ellipticity only.

Each weak $u_n$ is smooth in the interior. Here is the regularity argument. With a compactly supported space-time cutoff $\eta$, test its smooth divergence equation with $-D_{-h}(\eta^2D_hu_n)$, first using time averages to make the test legitimate. Difference-quotient integration by parts places $D_h$ on the coefficients and gradient. The principal term is at least $\lambda\|\eta D D_hu_n\|_2^2$. The remaining terms are sums of a bounded derivative of a smooth coefficient times a lower derivative of $u_n$, or a cutoff derivative times $D_hu_n$, or a differentiated smooth source; Cauchy–Schwarz and Young absorb half the principal term and bound the rest by a finite multiple of the $L^2_tH^1_x$ norm and source norms on a larger compact cylinder. A time cutoff removes its bottom boundary contribution; the top contribution has favorable sign. The quotient bound in [F4] and passage $h\to0$ give all second spatial derivatives locally in $L^2$. Repeating this calculation for a spatial derivative, with the Leibniz formula putting each differentiated coefficient beside a lower spatial derivative of $u_n$, proves inductively that every spatial derivative is locally in $L^2$. The equation then gives $u_{n,t}$ and all its spatial derivatives in $L^2$. Differentiating that equation distributionally in time gives all spatial derivatives of $u_{n,tt}$ in $L^2$, since the smooth coefficient time derivatives multiply already known spatial derivatives of $u_n$ and $u_{n,t}$. Induction gives all mixed time/space derivatives locally in $L^2$. Apply [F4] on a small spacetime simplex around each interior point, with arbitrarily high Sobolev order; its extension and embedding theorems apply in dimension $d+1\ge2$. The resulting representatives are smooth and agree on overlaps because they represent the same almost-everywhere function.

On each compact subcylinder, [F5], the uniform supremum bound and the uniform local coefficient/source Hölder bounds give uniform bounds for $u_n,Du_n,D^2u_n,u_{n,t}$ and their parabolic Hölder seminorms. Apply [F6] to these finitely many derivative families, then extract diagonally over a countable exhaustion of compact subcylinders. The limits of derivatives are derivatives of the limit by the coordinate segment integral identities. Thus a subsequence tends locally with two spatial and one time derivatives to $u$, and passage to the equations gives $Pu=f$. The uniform $\alpha$ seminorm bounds pass directly to differences of the limit, giving its asserted local full-$\alpha$ regularity. Its supremum is bounded by $\|\psi\|_\infty+T\|f\|_\infty$ after letting the uniform data approximation error decrease to zero.

Fix $(x_0,t_0)$ on the lateral face with $t_0>0$ and an error $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $\rho,\eta>0$ such that $H$ differs from $c_0=\psi(x_0,t_0)$ by less than $\varepsilon$ when $|x-x_0|<\rho$, $|t-t_0|<\eta$, also allowing $t=0$ if needed. Then $H_n$ differs by less than $2\varepsilon$ for all large $n$. On the local cylinder with bottom $s=\max(0,t_0-\eta)$ use $W=2\varepsilon+A h+B(t-t_0)^2$. Choose $B$ to dominate the uniform solution bound on the artificial bottom if $s>0$, using $B\eta^2$; if $s=0$ the initial data already have the required $2\varepsilon$ bound. Choose $A$ both to dominate on the artificial spatial face and to satisfy $A\ge M_f+\|q\|_\infty|c_0|+2B\eta$, increasing the uniform $q$ bound slightly if necessary. Then $(\partial_t-L_n)W\ge A-2B\eta$ dominates the absolute source of $u_n-c_0$, which includes the term $q_nc_0$. On the true boundary of $U_n$ its datum is $H_n$, so the comparison in step 1.2 gives $|u_n-c_0|\le W$ throughout this neighborhood. First pass to the interior limit, then let $(x,t)\to(x_0,t_0)$, and finally $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. This proves lateral boundary attainment from both time directions.

At $(x_0,0)$, including a corner, use $W=2\varepsilon+A|x-x_0|^2+Bt$. Choose $A$ to dominate on the artificial spatial face and choose $B\ge M_f+\|q\|_\infty|\psi(x_0,0)|+CA$, where $C$ bounds $|L_n|x-x_0|^2|$ on the neighborhood. The terms $-q_nW$ have favorable sign. Initial and nearby lateral data differ from $\psi(x_0,0)$ by at most $2\varepsilon$. The same comparison and limits prove initial attainment. At spatial interior points of the original final face, step 1.3 and step 5.1 give regularity and continuity. Together these arguments extend $u$ continuously to the whole closed cylinder with its prescribed values. Step 1.1 gives uniqueness.

If the original bounded divergence coefficients $a,b,c,d$ have the distributionally compatible expansion $A=a$, $\beta_j=\sum_iD_ia_{ij}+b_j+c_j$, $q=\sum_iD_ib_i+d$, choose their convolutions rather than independently convolving the expanded coefficients. Use a nonnegative temporal mollifier supported at strictly positive past lags, so its convolution samples $t-s$ with $s>0$, and a spatial mollifier whose support stays inside $U$ at every point of $U_n$. Extend in time by $a=\lambda I$, $b=c=d=0$ before time zero; this introduces no spatial derivative error. Distributional spatial differentiation commutes with convolution, so the expanded coefficients are the convolutions of $\beta,q$ and retain their bounds and sign. At $t\le T$ no value or limit of the original $b,c,d$ beyond or at $T$ is needed. Each fixed smooth approximant can be extended locally past $T$ when its existence construction requires it; only its convergence on positive-time compact sets below $T$ is needed for the energy limit. The boundary arguments apply at every lateral time below $T$, and the solution already constructed in step 7.1 supplies the continuous final trace. This proves the compatible approximation assertion without imposing endpoint continuity on the original divergence coefficients.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded, let $T>0$, and set $Q=U\times(0,T)$ and
$$\Gamma_T=(\bar U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T]).$$
The final-time face $U\times\{T\}$ is excluded from $\Gamma_T$. For time-dependent coefficients define
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^dD_i\bigl(a_{ij}(x,t)D_j u+b_i(x,t)u\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_i(x,t)D_i u+d(x,t)u.$$
Where the coefficient derivatives exist, write its nondivergence expansion as
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_i\widetilde b_iD_i u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
where $\widetilde b_i=\sum_jD_j a_{ij}+b_i+c_i$ and $\widetilde c=\sum_iD_i b_i+d$. The initial-boundary value problem uses the sign convention
$$-u_t+L_t[u]=f\quad\hbox{in }Q,\qquad u=\varphi\quad\hbox{on }\partial U\times[0,T],\qquad u=g\quad\hbox{on }\bar U\times\{0\},$$
with compatibility $g(x)=\varphi(x,0)$ on $\partial U$. Its residual for a trial function $h$ is $f+h_t-L_t[h]$, and its prescribed-data error is measured on $\Gamma_T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

derivations.claim:
Fix $t$. By [F4], approximate $e(\cdot,t)$ in $H^1(U)$ by compactly supported smooth functions. For each approximant the distributional definition of the divergence terms gives the spatial integration-by-parts identity; the coefficient bounds make every pairing continuous in $H^1$, so passing to the limit produces no boundary term because $e(\cdot,t)\in H^1_0(U)$. Integrate $-e_t+L_t[e]=r$ against $e$ and use [F1] and [F2]. Moving the time derivative to the left gives
$$\tfrac12 E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le (\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty)\|e(t)\|_2\|\nabla e(t)\|_2+\|d\|_\infty E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2\|e(t)\|_2,$$
where $E(t)=\|e(t)\|_2^2$.

By Young's inequality, the first product on the right is at most $\frac{\lambda_0}{4}\|\nabla e\|_2^2+C_1E(t)$ and the last product is at most $\frac12\|r(t)\|_2^2+\frac12E(t)$, for a finite $C_1$ depending only on the coefficient bounds and $\lambda_0$. Hence for $C_2=C_1+\|d\|_\infty+\frac12$,
$$E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le 2C_2E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2^2.$$

Dropping the nonnegative gradient term in step 1.2 and multiplying by $e^{-2C_2t}$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-2C_2t}E(t))\le e^{-2C_2t}\|r(t)\|_2^2$. Integrating from $0$ to any $s\le T$ yields
$$\sup_{0\le s\le T}E(s)\le e^{2C_2T}\left(E(0)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2\right).$$

Integrating step 1.2 from $0$ to $T$ and using step 2.1 gives
$$\lambda_0\int_0^T\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2dt\le E(0)+2C_2T\sup_{0\le t\le T}E(t)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2.$$
Combining this with step 2.1 and dividing by $\lambda_0>0$ proves the stated estimate after increasing the constant.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

derivations.claim: For almost every $t$, by [F4], approximate $e(\cdot,t)$ in $H^1(U)$ by compactly supported smooth functions. For each approximant the distributional definition of the divergence terms gives the spatial integration-by-parts identity; the coefficient bounds make every pairing continuous in $H^1$, so passing to the limit produces no boundary term because $e(\cdot,t)\in H^1_0(U)$. Pair the weak equation $-e_t+L_t[e]=r$ against $e$ in $V^*,V$ and use [F1] and [F2]. Moving the time derivative to the left gives $$\tfrac12 E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le (\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty)\|e(t)\|_2\|\nabla e(t)\|_2+\|d\|_\infty E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2\|e(t)\|_2,$$ where $E(t)=\|e(t)\|_2^2$.

By Young's inequality, the first product on the right is at most $\frac{\lambda_0}{4}\|\nabla e\|_2^2+C_1E(t)$ and the last product is at most $\frac12\|r(t)\|_2^2+\frac12E(t)$, for a finite $C_1$ depending only on the coefficient bounds and $\lambda_0$. Hence for $C_2=C_1+\|d\|_\infty+\frac12$, $$E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le 2C_2E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2^2.$$

Dropping the nonnegative gradient term in step 2.1 and multiplying by $e^{-2C_2t}$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-2C_2t}E(t))\le e^{-2C_2t}\|r(t)\|_2^2$. Integrating from $0$ to any $s\le T$ yields $$\sup_{0\le s\le T}E(s)\le e^{2C_2T}\left(E(0)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2\right).$$

Integrating step 2.1 from $0$ to $T$ and using step 3.1 gives $$\lambda_0\int_0^T\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2dt\le E(0)+2C_2T\sup_{0\le t\le T}E(t)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2.$$ Combining this with step 3.1 and dividing by $\lambda_0>0$ proves the stated estimate after increasing the constant.
