The **positive divergence convention** here means that the principal part is $+\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_j u)$. This sign is part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.

Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
On every ball, $C^{2,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ therefore agrees with the finite-scaled-norm class of that dependency. This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $m\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and $r\ge1$ be integers, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$
be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a $C^r$ map with

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

**Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice** ([[def-dependent-choice]]). Let
$(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space.

1. If $X$ is normal ([[def-normal-and-t4-spaces]]), $A \subseteq X$ is closed
   ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]) and $a \le b$ are reals, then every
   continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) extends to a continuous
   $F : X \to [a,b]$ with $F|_A = f$.
2. Conversely, if for every closed $A \subseteq X$ and every reals $a \le b$
   every continuous $f : A \to [a,b]$ extends to a continuous $F : X \to [a,b]$
   with $F|_A = f$, then $X$ is normal. **This direction uses no choice
   principle.**

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1\le p<\infty$, and let
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ admit a representative
$\tilde u\in C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then, with $T$ the trace operator
of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]],
$$Tu=\tilde u|_{\partial\Omega}\qquad\text{in }L^p(\partial\Omega);$$
in particular $Tu=0$ whenever such a representative vanishes on
$\partial\Omega$. Two representatives continuous on $\overline\Omega$ of the
same class have the same restriction to $\partial\Omega$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$. For $u,v\ge0$,
$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix $n\ge2$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Consider a family of bounded smooth domains $V$ in a fixed bounded set with a common finite boundary graph atlas: the graph radii, inverse-chart radii and bounds for all chart and inverse-chart derivatives through order two and the $\alpha$-Hölder seminorms of their second derivatives are uniformly controlled. Let $L=A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+c$ have real smooth coefficients near $\bar V$, with $A=A^T$, $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$ for fixed $0<\lambda\le\Lambda$, and uniformly bounded global $C^{0,\alpha}(\bar V)$ coefficient norms. There is a uniform $C<\infty$ such that every real $u\in C^\infty(\bar V)$ with zero boundary values satisfies
$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar V)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;V}+\|Lu\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\bar V)}\bigr).$$
The constant depends only on the stated uniform geometric and coefficient controls, dimension and exponent, and not on higher smoothness norms. No sign of $c$ is required for this a priori estimate.

Furthermore every nonempty bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ has smooth bounded open subsets $V_j$ with $\bar V_j\subset U$, every compact subset of $U$ eventually contained in $V_j$, and a common finite graph atlas with the uniform controls just described. Nestedness is not asserted or required.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

Let $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ be a finite linearly independent list in a real or complex inner product space. There is an orthonormal list $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ such that, for every $k\le r$,

$$\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{k-1})=\operatorname{span}(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}).$$

It is obtained recursively from

$$u_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j,\qquad e_k=\frac{u_k}{\lVert u_k\rVert}.$$

For $r=0$, both lists are empty.

If $(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$ is a finite orthonormal list and $v$ is any vector, then

$$\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2\le\lVert v\rVert^2.$$

Equality holds exactly when $v\in\operatorname{span}(e_0,\ldots,e_{r-1})$. If the list is an orthonormal basis, then for all $v,w$,

$$v=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i,\qquad \langle v,w\rangle=\sum_{i<r}\langle v,e_i\rangle\overline{\langle w,e_i\rangle},$$

and

$$\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{i<r}|\langle v,e_i\rangle|^2.$$

The empty-list case is included.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

derivations.claim: Expand the intended divergence expression by the product rule to obtain $L=A:D^2+\beta\cdot D+\gamma$. On a bounded Lipschitz domain, two sufficiently close points in a fixed smaller graph patch can be joined inside a larger patch by a path of length at most a fixed multiple of their distance; bounded first derivatives therefore give a Lipschitz bound for $a,b$ there. A finite cover and the supremum bound for separated pairs give their global Hölder bounds. Thus the finite global coefficient assumptions give finite Hölder bounds for the expanded coefficients, $\gamma\le0$, and a finite bound for $DA$. Throughout the proof write $c=\gamma$, and use $\lambda=\lambda_0$, $\Lambda=\Lambda_0$.

If $n=1$, the bounded Lipschitz set is a finite union of open intervals: its compact boundary has a finite one-sided graph-chart cover, and in dimension one each such chart contains one boundary point. On each interval $(a,b)$ all coefficients and $f$ extend Hölder-continuously to $[a,b]$ and $A\ge\lambda$. Write $y=(u,u')$, so $y'=M(x)y+F(x)$, where $M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-c/A&-\beta/A\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $F=(0,f/A)$. For $Th(x)=\int_a^xM(t)h(t)\,dt$, iterated integration gives $\|T^kh\|_\infty\le \|h\|_\infty(\|M\|_\infty(b-a))^k/k!$. Therefore the uniformly convergent series $y=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k(y(a)+\int_a^{\cdot}F)$ solves the integral equation, hence the differential system; the factorial bound also proves uniqueness by iterating the homogeneous difference equation. Choose one particular solution with the prescribed left value and slope zero, and add $s$ times the homogeneous solution with initial value zero and slope one. That homogeneous solution cannot also vanish at $b$: otherwise [F2] would make it identically zero, contradicting its slope at $a$. Thus exactly one $s$ gives the prescribed right value. The equation makes $u''$ globally Hölder, so $u\in C^{2,\alpha}([a,b])$. Zero endpoint values imply $u\in H^1_0(a,b)$ directly: multiply by a cutoff vanishing within $\varepsilon$ of each endpoint, with derivative bounded by $C/\varepsilon$; since $|u|\le\|u'\|_\infty\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial(a,b))$, the cutoff error in $H^1$ tends to zero, and each compactly supported $H^1$ function is approximated by mollification. For zero data, integration against $u$ gives $\lambda\|u'\|_2^2\le\|f\|_2\|u\|_2+\|\beta-A'\|_\infty\|u'\|_2\|u\|_2+\|c\|_\infty\|u\|_2^2$; Young's inequality and [F2] then give the stated energy bound on these finitely many intervals. This proves all existence, energy, and global regularity conclusions in dimension one; [F2] gives stability. Henceforth take $n\ge2$.

Let $\delta(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus U)$ on all of $\mathbb R^n$; it is nonnegative, 1-Lipschitz, vanishes outside $U$, and has compact support because $U$ is bounded. Fix a nonnegative unit-mass smooth mollifier supported in the unit ball. Put $\varepsilon_j\downarrow0$ and $\delta_j=\rho_{\varepsilon_j}*\delta$. Then $$|\delta_j-\delta|\le\varepsilon_j.$$ Choose a regular value $t_j\in(2\varepsilon_j,3\varepsilon_j)$, using the local Euclidean Morse–Sard theorem, and set $V_j=\{\delta_j>t_j\}$. This is bounded with compact smooth boundary, satisfies $\bar V_j\subset U$ (indeed $\delta\ge t_j-\varepsilon_j>\varepsilon_j$ on its closure), and contains $\{\delta>4\varepsilon_j\}$. Every compact subset of $U$ is contained in $V_j$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Discard an initial empty $V_j$ if necessary. Nestedness is not required anywhere below. If there are several components, use the same argument componentwise; a compact smooth boundary has a finite graph cover and the proof supplies the same finite-cover regularity on their union.

Choose $s_j<\varepsilon_j/4$ tending to zero and mollify the original coefficients and forcing at scale $s_j$ on a neighborhood of $\bar V_j$: $$A_j=\rho_{s_j}*A,\quad\beta_j=\rho_{s_j}*\beta,\quad c_j=\rho_{s_j}*c,\quad f_j=\rho_{s_j}*f.$$ Only values inside $U$ are used there. Consequently $A_j=A_j^T$, $\lambda I\le A_j\le\Lambda I$, $c_j\le0$, and the sup bounds of $\beta_j,c_j,f_j,DA_j$ do not exceed the original corresponding bounds. On every fixed interior ball, their Hölder norms are uniformly bounded and they converge uniformly to the original coefficients/data; $DA_j\to DA$ uniformly locally as well. The Hölder bound follows directly by integrating $|F(x-z)-F(y-z)|\le[F]_\alpha|x-y|^\alpha$. Each coefficient is smooth near $\bar V_j$; its higher derivatives can grow with $j$, which does not matter.

Extend $g$ to a bounded continuous $G$ on $\mathbb R^n$ using Tietze and set $G_j=\rho_{s_j}*G$. Uniform convergence $G_j\to G$ holds on any fixed compact neighborhood of $\bar U$, by uniform continuity there. Also $\|G_j\|_\infty\le\|G\|_\infty$. The lemma gives a smooth classical $u_j$ on $\bar V_j$ satisfying $$L_ju_j=f_j\quad\hbox{in }V_j,\qquad u_j=G_j\quad\hbox{on }\partial V_j.$$

Take a slab $a\le x_1\le b$ containing $\bar U$, put $B=\sup_j\|\beta_{j,1}\|_\infty$, $C_0=\sup_j\|c_j\|_\infty$, and choose $\kappa$ with $\lambda\kappa^2-B\kappa-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi=e^{\kappa x_1}$, $L_j\psi\ge e^{\kappa a}=:\eta>0$. Fix $M>e^{\kappa b}$ and put $\Phi=M-\psi>0$. Then $L_j\Phi\le-\eta$ for every $j$.

Let $Q=\|G\|_\infty$ and $R=\|f\|_\infty$. On $\partial V_j$, both $u_j-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$ and $-u_j-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$ are nonpositive. Their $L_j$ images are nonnegative, since $c_j\le0$, $|f_j|\le R$ and $L_j\Phi\le-\eta$. Comparison gives $$|u_j|\le Q+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_\infty=:M_0$$ on $V_j$. This constant depends only on the original domain/slab, uniform ellipticity and expanded coefficient sup bounds, $R,Q$. It is independent of $j$, of the smoothness of $\partial V_j$, and of all higher coefficient derivatives.

For every ball $B_{2r}(x)\Subset U$, it is contained in $V_j$ for large $j$. Apply the actual interior Schauder theorem to $u_j$ there. All coefficient $C^\alpha$ norms and ellipticity constants are uniformly controlled on that fixed ball, $\|u_j\|_\infty\le M_0$, and the $C^\alpha$ norm of $f_j$ is uniformly bounded. Hence $u_j$ is uniformly bounded in $C^{2,\alpha}(B_r(x))$.

Cover $U$ by a countable family of such inner balls with rational centers/radii. Arzelà–Ascoli on each smaller closed ball and diagonal extraction give one subsequence for which $(u_j,Du_j,D^2u_j)$ converges uniformly on every compact subset of $U$. The fundamental theorem of calculus on coordinate segments identifies the limits with $(u,Du,D^2u)$; their compatibility on overlapping balls follows from uniform convergence. Passing each Hessian Hölder difference quotient to the limit proves $u\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Uniform local convergence of all coefficients/data and derivatives gives $Lu=f$ pointwise. The uniform bound gives $|u|\le M_0$.

Fix $q\in\partial U$. Let $B_R(z)$ be an exterior ball tangent at $q$. Replace it by the smaller ball with center $z'=(z+q)/2$ and radius $r_0=R/2$. Its **closed** ball is contained in $B_R(z)\cup\{q\}$: for $x\ne q$ on the smaller closed ball, strict triangle inequality gives $|x-z|<R$. Thus $$|x-z'|\ge r_0\quad(x\in\bar U),\qquad |x-z'|=r_0\iff x=q.$$ This strict contact property is necessary; the original exterior ball could touch the boundary at several points.

Write $r=|x-z'|$, $e=(x-z')/r$, and let $R_1=\max_{\bar U}r$. Choose an integer $m>0$ so large that $$(m+2)\lambda-n\Lambda-R_1\sup_j\|\beta_j\|_\infty\ge1.$$ Define $W_0=r_0^{-m}-r^{-m}$. It is smooth near $\bar U$, nonnegative there, vanishes exactly at $q$, and a direct differentiation gives $$L_jW_0=m r^{-m-2}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}A_j-(m+2)e^TA_je+r\beta_j\cdot e\bigr)+c_jW_0\le-mr^{-m-2}\le-mR_1^{-m-2}.$$ After multiplying by $R_1^{m+2}/m$, obtain a single $W_q\ge0$ with $W_q(q)=0$, $W_q>0$ on $\bar U\setminus\{q\}$, and $L_jW_q\le-1$ for every $j$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded, let $T>0$, and set $Q=U\times(0,T)$ and
$$\Gamma_T=(\bar U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T]).$$
The final-time face $U\times\{T\}$ is excluded from $\Gamma_T$. For time-dependent coefficients define
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^dD_i(a_{ij}(x,t)D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i(x,t)u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_i(x,t)D_i u+d(x,t)u.$$
Where the coefficient derivatives exist, write its nondivergence expansion as
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_i\widetilde b_iD_i u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
where $\widetilde b_i=\sum_jD_j a_{ji}+b_i+c_i$ and $\widetilde c=\sum_iD_i b_i+d$. For symmetric $a$, the drift also equals $\sum_jD_j a_{ij}+b_i+c_i$, the form used by the symmetric source consumers. The initial-boundary value problem uses the sign convention
$$-u_t+L_t[u]=f\quad\hbox{in }Q,\qquad u=\varphi\quad\hbox{on }\partial U\times[0,T],\qquad u=g\quad\hbox{on }\bar U\times\{0\},$$
with compatibility $g(x)=\varphi(x,0)$ on $\partial U$. Its residual for a trial function $h$ is $f+h_t-L_t[h]$, and its prescribed-data error is measured on $\Gamma_T$.

For the source notation $C_{2+\alpha}(Q)$, use the parabolic distance
$$d_p((x,t),(y,s))=(|x-y|^2+|t-s|)^{1/2}.$$
Let $B=U\times\{0\}$ and $S_\tau=\partial U\times[0,\tau]$. For $P=(x,\tau)\in Q$, set $\delta(P)=\inf_{R\in B\cup S_\tau}d_p(P,R)$ and $\delta_{P,Q}=\min\{\delta(P),\delta(Q)\}$. For an integer $m\ge0$, define
$$|v|_{m,\alpha}=\sup_{P\in Q}\delta(P)^m|v(P)|+\sup_{P\ne Q\in Q}\delta_{P,Q}^{m+\alpha}\frac{|v(P)-v(Q)|}{d_p(P,Q)^\alpha}.$$
The class $C_{2+\alpha}(Q)$ consists of functions for which
$$|u|_{0,\alpha}+\sum_i|D_i u|_{1,\alpha}+\sum_{i,j}|D_{ij}u|_{1,\alpha}+|u_t|_{2,\alpha}<\infty,$$
with the indicated derivatives continuous in $Q$. This fixes the source's weighted parabolic Hölder convention.

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded and open, $T>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. At every $x_0\in\partial U$ assume there is an exterior tangent closed ball, disjoint from $U$ and containing $x_0$ on its sphere. Let $A=A^T$, $\beta,q,f$ be bounded on $U\times(0,T]$, locally parabolic $\alpha$-Hölder up to its final face, with $\lambda I\le A\le\Lambda I$, $\lambda>0$, and $q\le0$. Moreover it is the interior limit of smooth-coefficient weak solutions on finite polyhedral subdomains exhausting $U$, with uniform supremum bounds and the uniform compact-interior estimates just stated. If the coefficients possess a bounded divergence representation compatible in distributions, those approximants may be chosen by convolution of its original divergence coefficients.

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open with an exterior tangent ball at every boundary point, and let $T>0$. Consider the intended divergence operator
$$L_tu=\sum_{i,j}D_i(a_{ij}D_ju)+\sum_iD_i(b_iu)+\sum_i c_iD_iu+du.$$
